title: Tiny 1.7-Billion-Year-Old Fossils Could Unlock the Secret of How Complex Life Began
summary: Have you ever wondered how life on Earth went from tiny, invisible germs to giant dinosaurs, towering trees, and you? Scientists just found a big clue: fossils that are 1.7 billion years old! That's way before dinosaurs, before fish, even before most things you can see. These fossils are so small you'd need a microscope to see them, but they might be the oldest complex cells ever discovered. Complex cells, called eukaryotes (say: yoo-KAIR-ee-oats), are the building blocks of all plants, animals, and fungi. Unlike simple bacteria, eukaryotes have a special compartment inside called a nucleus that holds their DNA, like a safe for instructions. They also have tiny power plants called mitochondria that give them energy to grow bigger and do more. For almost 90% of Earth's history, only simple microbes existed. Then, around 1.7 billion years ago, these complex cells appeared. But how did they evolve? That's the mystery. The new fossils, found in ancient rocks from Canada, might be early eukaryotes. They look like tiny spheres with little tails, and some have strange bumps. Scientists think these bumps could be the remains of a process where one cell swallowed another and they became partners—a huge step toward complex life. Finding such old, soft cells is super rare because they usually rot away. But these were preserved in a special kind of rock that formed in an ancient ocean. Now, researchers are studying the fossils' chemistry to learn more. If these really are early eukaryotes, it means complex life started earlier than we thought, and that could help us understand if life on other planets might become complex too. So next time you look at a tree or your pet, remember: it all started with tiny cells like these, billions of years ago.
why_it_matters: Learning about the first complex cells helps us understand where all living things, including you and your pets, came from.
